publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The claim that cognitive control requires awareness, and the inconsistent evidence about whether unconscious events can trigger it.
span.quote: Recent research suggests, however, that several behavioral phenomena that have been construed as instances of cognitive control can be prompted by events of which actors are not aware.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: While the former type of control seems to work outside of awareness, the latter type of control seems to be restricted to consciously registered events that call for control.

span.label: cognitive control triggered by unconscious events
span.quote: Instead, we believe that the important and empirically testable question is whether changes of behavior through cognitive control occur when the control-invoking event remains unnoticed.

span.label: review
span.quote: Here we give a brief review of this research, discuss possible reasons for inconsistencies in the empirical evidence, and suggest some lines of future research.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: implicit control cues must leave a memory trace that survives across trials, and only consciously represented events are strong enough to bridge that interval, so unconscious implicit cues never reach the control system
span.quote: Only conscious event representations might be strong enough to bridge longer time intervals.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: adapting to a statistical property such as conflict frequency requires accumulating information across many separate episodes over a long period, an accumulation that unconscious representations cannot support
span.quote: In these cases information of several such events has to be accumulated over a long period of time, and over a certain number of such events to extract, for example, the proportion of incongruent trials.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: control is executed by if-then plans; explicit cues let participants specify both sides of the plan in advance, whereas implicit events leave the if-side and then-side vague, so the plan itself has to be revised and it is this revision that demands awareness
span.quote: It seems that, for example, adaptation to response conflict requires a specification or correction of if-then plans, and perhaps it is exactly this alteration of plans that requires awareness.

span.label: The proposed resolution: control cued by a single explicit signal can be triggered without awareness, while control that has to be inferred from a pattern of events cannot
span.quote: While the former type of control seems to work outside of awareness, the latter type of control seems to be restricted to consciously registered events that call for control.

span.label: An implicit cue is one where the environment never signals the need for control - it merely suggests it, so the actor must infer it
span.quote: Cognitive control invoked by implicit events Conflict frequency The need for control is sometimes not explicitly signaled, but is merely implicitly suggested, by the environment.

span.label: Unconscious stimuli are processed only where the system was prepared in advance to process them, so preparation rather than awareness does the work
span.quote: Thus, the effectiveness of subliminal stimuli depends on preparatory processes that occur in advance of, and set the stage for, such subliminal stimuli.

span.label: Conflict adaptation works by reallocating attention toward the relevant stimulus aspects after conflict is frequent or recent
span.quote: The crucial observation is that when response-conflict is generally frequent (e.g., in a block of trials), or has just been expe-rienced (e.g., in the preceding trial), the information processing is altered in subsequent trials, such that, for example, more attention is devoted to task-relevant rather than to task-irrelevant stimulus aspects.

span.label: An indirect route could fake unconscious control: the prime stays unconscious while its behavioural consequences do not, and the actor adjusts to those
span.quote: For example, the proportion of incongruent masked primes may remain undetected, but the resulting increase of error rates may be noticed and may prompt a corresponding adjustment indirectly (cf. Jaśkowski et al., 2003 ).

span.label: The review's own headline result is that the literature it surveys does not settle the question.
span.quote: To anticipate a main result, the outcome of this research program is ambiguous.

span.label: The evidence base the review rests on may be distorted by selective publication of positive findings.
span.quote: Second, research on the consciousness-control link is perhaps particularly susceptible to publication bias.

span.label: The authors name publication bias in their own literature: positive evidence for control without awareness is publishable and negative evidence is not
span.quote: Second, research on the consciousness-control link is perhaps particularly susceptible to publication bias. Positive evidence for control without awareness is exciting and may make it easier to be published in prestigious journals (or to be published at all), while negative evidence resides in less prestigious journals (or may not be published).

span.label: The effects at issue are small, so studies claiming them need power that is not always present
span.quote: First, effects of unconscious stimuli are often small. Therefore, studies aiming to show such effects must have sufficient power to do so.

span.label: The central claim is stated with an epistemic hedge: awareness seems essential, or else the evidence is merely not consistent
span.quote: However, if an event such as recent or frequent response conflict merely implicitly suggests the need of cognitive control, awareness of this event seems essential, or at least, evidence for the induction of control phenomena without awareness is not consistently found.

span.label: The failures of implicit control might be failures of the manipulation rather than of the capacity
span.quote: For example, there might be adaptation to unconsciously induced response conflict, but sometimes the subliminally induced conflict was too small.

span.label: The key term is admitted to be poorly defined
span.quote: Although not very well defined, it seems fair to say that cognitive control denotes those processes that configure the cognitive system to process stimuli in a specific manner, and re-configure the cognitive system when certain events tell the observer/actor to treat stimuli in a different way.

span.label: control cue - EXPLICIT: a single stimulus that directly signals what to do, such as a task cue or stop signal - and this kind works without awareness
span.quote: Specifically, we suggest to differentiate cognitive control evoked either because of explicit or because of implicit control cues.

span.label: control cue - IMPLICIT: no signal at all, only a pattern in the environment from which the need for control must be inferred - and this kind appears to need awareness
span.quote: Cognitive control invoked by implicit events Conflict frequency The need for control is sometimes not explicitly signaled, but is merely implicitly suggested, by the environment.

span.label: the claim - as a positive necessity: awareness is essential for implicitly cued control
span.quote: However, if an event such as recent or frequent response conflict merely implicitly suggests the need of cognitive control, awareness of this event seems essential, or at least, evidence for the induction of control phenomena without awareness is not consistently found.

span.label: the claim - as an absence of evidence: the effect has simply not been found consistently, which is a weaker statement the authors deliberately keep in reserve
span.quote: It is possible that there are conditions that prevented the discovery of implicit control, although it is possible in principle.

span.label: unconscious effect - genuinely unconscious: the masked event itself drives the adjustment
span.quote: Although the prime is heavily masked, and thus phenomenally “unaware”, it leaves a trace in behavior: Responses are usually faster and more accurate when prime and target are mapped to the same motor response

span.label: unconscious effect - indirectly conscious: the event stays unconscious but its behavioural consequences are noticed, and the actor adjusts to those
span.quote: Masked events as such may remain unconscious, but their side-effects in behavior become apparent by self-observation.

span.label: claim_type: mechanism
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: mechanism — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Specifically, we suggest to differentiate cognitive control evoked either because of explicit or because of implicit control cues.

span.label: extends → Crump et al. (2006) and Crump, Vaquero, & Milliken (2008) on context-specific proportion congruency effects
span.quote: This finding qualifies observations by Crump and colleagues ( Crump et al., 2006 ; Crump, Vaquero, & Milliken, 2008 ).

span.label: critiques → Dehaene and Naccache's workspace model, which reserves cognitive control for consciousness
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHICH PROCESSES NEED CONSCIOUSNESS. 'DEHAENE AND NACCACHE (2001) SUGGEST IN THEIR WORKSPACE MODEL THAT ROUTINE ACTIONS ARE POSSIBLE WITHOUT CONSCIOUSNESS, WHILE CONSCIOUSNESS IS REQUIRED FOR COGNITIVE CONTROL.' The model is stated precisely enough to be tested and the critique targets exactly the line it draws - so the disagreement is about WHERE the boundary falls, not whether there is one. Q-505.
span.quote: Similarly, Dehaene and Naccache ( 2001 ) suggest in their workspace model that routine actions are possible without consciousness, while consciousness is required for cognitive control.

span.label: critiques → Jack and Shallice's separation of conscious from automatic action
span.quote: For example, Jack and Shallice ( 2001 ) emphasize that the underlying processes engaged by conscious action are different from those engaged by automatic action.

span.label: extends → preparation accounts of subliminal processing, on which unconscious stimuli work only where the system is set up for them
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS AN ASSUMED PRECONDITION. 'EXPLANATIONS OF VISION WITHOUT AWARENESS TYPICALLY ASSUME THAT EVEN UNCONSCIOUS STIMULI ARE PROCESSED, PROVIDED THE COGNITIVE SYSTEM WAS PREPARED IN ADVANCE TO DO SO.' Unconscious processing is granted only where the system was set up for it, so a null in an unprepared condition is not evidence against unconscious processing - it is outside the claim. Q-511.
span.quote: Explanations of vision without awareness typically assume that even unconscious stimuli are processed, provided the cognitive system was prepared in advance to do so (e.g., Ansorge & Neumann, 2005 ; Kiesel, 2009 ; Kiesel, Kunde, & Hoffmann, 2007 ; Kunde, Kiesel, & Hoffmann, 2003 , 2005 ; Martens & Kiefer, 2009 ; Neumann & Klotz, 1994 ; Pohl, Kiesel, Kunde, & Hoffmann, 2010 ).

span.label: conflict frequency —causes→ cognitive control
span.quote: The crucial observation is that when response-conflict is generally frequent (e.g., in a block of trials), or has just been expe-rienced (e.g., in the preceding trial), the information processing is altered in subsequent trials, such that, for example, more attention is devoted to task-relevant rather than to task-irrelevant stimulus aspects.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE DIRECTION IS INVERTED AND THE CLAIM IS ATTRIBUTED) · task switching —part-of→ cognitive control
span.note: RETRACTED: THE DIRECTION IS INVERTED AND THE CLAIM IS ATTRIBUTED. The edge is `task switching --part-of--> cognitive control`. The span: 'in studies on task switching, participants have to respond to the same stimuli in a different way depending on the currently instructed task context, and thus COGNITIVE CONTROL IS BELIEVED TO BE HEAVILY INVOLVED IN TASK SWITCHING'. The sentence says CONTROL IS INVOLVED IN SWITCHING - the paradigm engages the faculty. The edge says the paradigm is a component of the faculty, which is the other way round; and `is believed` marks it as the field's view rather than this paper's finding. Q-431. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: For example, in studies on task switching, participants have to respond to the same stimuli in a different way depending on the currently instructed task context, and thus cognitive control is believed to be heavily involved in task switching ( Kiesel et al., 2010 ; Monsell, 2003 ).

span.label: stop-signal —part-of→ cognitive control
span.quote: Here, the time interval between the occurrence of a certain instruction stimulus (e.g., a task cue or a stop-signal), and the point in time when the impact of cognitive control becomes apparent (mostly by responses to a certain stimulus) is barely longer than a few hundred milliseconds, and accumulation of know-ledge over several explicit events is not necessary.

span.label: conflict frequency —part-of→ interference tasks
span.quote: Such conflicting tendencies are a hallmark of so-called interference tasks , such as the Simon task ( Simon, 1969 ), the Eriksen task ( Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974 ), or the Stroop task ( Stroop, 1935 ).

span.label: subliminal priming —part-of→ prime stimulus
span.quote: In subliminal priming experiments, participants respond to a target that is preceded by another, so-called prime stimulus .

span.label: blindsight —distinct-from→ consciousness
span.quote: Classical demonstrations of this phenomenon relate to neurological cases of blindsight, neglect, or extinction, where patients, despite being unaware of parts of their visual field, locate and identify stimuli above chance level (e.g., Fuentes & Humphreys, 1996 ; Pöppel, Held, & Frost, 1973 ; Weiskrantz, 1986 , 2002 ; Young & de Haan, 1993 ).

span.label: workspace model —operationalised-as→ consciousness
span.quote: Similarly, Dehaene and Naccache ( 2001 ) suggest in their workspace model that routine actions are possible without consciousness, while consciousness is required for cognitive control.

span.label: automatic action —contrasted-with→ cognitive control
span.quote: For example, Jack and Shallice ( 2001 ) emphasize that the underlying processes engaged by conscious action are different from those engaged by automatic action.

span.label: publication bias —causes→ consciousness
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak
span.quote: Second, research on the consciousness-control link is perhaps particularly susceptible to publication bias.

span.label: post-error slowing —part-of→ cognitive control
span.quote: ( 2009 ) observed that another instance of cognitive control, post-error slowing, did not occur.

span.label: subliminal priming —distinct-from→ consciousness
span.quote: Despite such differences, all these models share common ground: Stimulus awareness is not necessary for processing, given that the observer/actor is prepared to encounter these stimuli (e.g., Dehaene & Naccache, 2001 ).

span.label: speed-accuracy function —operationalised-as→ cognitive control
span.quote: shifts along the speed-accuracy function be prompted subliminally by explicit cues?

span.label: When the need for control is signalled by a single explicit cue, that cue does not have to be consciously perceived for control to be recruited.
span.quote: If the need for control is conveyed by an explicit event, awareness of that event is dispensable.

span.label: When the need for control is only implied by recent or frequent response conflict, awareness of that event appears to be necessary, and unconscious induction of control is not reliably obtained.
span.quote: However, if an event such as recent or frequent response conflict merely implicitly suggests the need of cognitive control, awareness of this event seems essential, or at least, evidence for the induction of control phenomena without awareness is not consistently found.

span.label: Exactly three control functions have so far been shown to be triggerable by subliminal explicit cues: task preparation, response inhibition, and orienting of attention.
span.quote: These are task preparation, response inhibition, and orienting of attention.

span.label: Masked primes reliably activate task sets, facilitating the cued task and even biasing which task is freely chosen.
span.quote: In sum, there is little doubt that masked stimuli have the power to induce task sets.

span.label: Strategic adaptation to how often conflict occurs is obtained only when the conflicting irrelevant information is consciously seen.
span.quote: Importantly, such strategic adaptation to conflict frequency occurs only when the irre-levant information is consciously perceived

span.label: Conflict adaptation requires that the prime in the preceding trial was visible, yet the control settings so established still act on masked primes in the current trial - so awareness is needed to invoke control, not to execute it.
span.quote: This observation implies that prime visibility is necessary to invoke cognitive control, whereas the control processes that alter information processing can operate on masked stimuli as well.

span.label: Context-specific proportion-congruency adaptation appeared with visible primes but disappeared with subliminal primes, whose overall congruency effect was unaffected by the context cue.
span.quote: Importantly in contrast to the results of Experiment 1, this congruency effect was not affected by context information.

span.label: Taken as a whole the literature is inconsistent: some experiments show control prompted by unnoticed events and others show it fails.
span.quote: Some studies suggest that cognitive control can be prompted by events that remain unnoticed, whereas other studies suggest that they cannot.

span.label: The authors argue that cognitive control itself does not depend on the actor having meta-knowledge about when or how control is being applied.
span.quote: We conjecture that cognitive control does not require meta-knowledge of when and how to apply it.

span.label: control cued by a single explicit signal appears to work without awareness; control that must be inferred from a pattern does not
span.quote: While the former type of control seems to work outside of awareness, the latter type of control seems to be restricted to consciously registered events that call for control.

span.label: masked primes speed and improve responses when mapped to the same response or category as the target
span.quote: Although the prime is heavily masked, and thus phenomenally “unaware”, it leaves a trace in behavior: Responses are usually faster and more accurate when prime and target are mapped to the same motor response

span.label: the literature on unconscious control is inconsistent, and the authors treat that inconsistency as the thing to be explained
span.quote: Here we give a brief review of this research, discuss possible reasons for inconsistencies in the empirical evidence, and suggest some lines of future research.

span.label: the field may be shaped by publication bias favouring positive evidence for unconscious control
span.quote: Positive evidence for control without awareness is exciting and may make it easier to be published in prestigious journals (or to be published at all), while negative evidence resides in less prestigious journals (or may not be published).

span.label: cognitive control
span.quote: Although not very well defined, it seems fair to say that cognitive control denotes those processes that configure the cognitive system to process stimuli in a specific manner, and re-configure the cognitive system when certain events tell the observer/actor to treat stimuli in a different way.

span.label: explicit (control-invoking) events
span.quote: Explicit events consist of one distinct stimulus that directly informs the observer what is requested from him or her.

span.label: implicit (control-invoking) events
span.quote: In contrast, implicit events encompass more than one single, explicit stimulus and they have to be derived from the task environment.

span.label: prime stimulus / subliminal priming experiment
span.quote: In subliminal priming experiments, participants respond to a target that is preceded by another, so-called prime stimulus

span.label: Gratton effect (conflict adaptation)
span.quote: The typical finding, sometimes called the Gratton effect ( Gratton et al., 1992 ), is a reduction of congruency effects in trials that directly follow an incongruent (conflict-laden) trial in interference tasks.

span.label: interference tasks
span.quote: In these tasks, a nominally task-irrelevant stimulus or stimulus feature suggests a different response than is actually required.

span.label: cognitive control
span.quote: cognitive control denotes those processes that configure the cognitive system to process stimuli in a specific manner, and re-configure the cognitive system when certain events tell the observer/actor to treat stimuli in a different way

span.label: subliminal priming
span.quote: In subliminal priming experiments, participants respond to a target that is preceded by another, so-called prime stimulus .

span.label: 54 ms ... 32 ms — size of the congruency effect with visible primes in the low-interference versus high-interference context, showing context-specific adaptation
span.quote: The congruency effect amounted to 54 ms in the low-interference context, and to 32 ms in the high-interference context.

span.label: 80% — proportion of congruent trials in the low-interference colour context and of incongruent trials in the high-interference colour context
span.quote: For one color, trials were mostly (80%) congruent (low-interference context), whereas with the other color trials were mostly (80%) incongruent (high-interference context).

span.label: 80% ... 20% — proportions of congruent trials in the two conditions across which masked priming effects declined
span.quote: found that masked priming effects declined from a condition with 80% congruent trials to a condition with 20% congruent trials
